cards.name: Dunford’s 5-Component Positioning Framework
cards.diagnostic: If our solution ceased to exist tomorrow, what specific alternatives would customers use, and what distinct value do our unique capabilities deliver over those alternatives?
artifact: A 5-column positioning ledger: Competitive Alternatives → Unique Capabilities → Quantified Value Drivers → Ideal Customer Profile (ICP) Segments → Category Framing.
cards.trap: Declaring that no direct competitors exist, or positioning into ill-defined space, deprives buyers of an evaluative frame.
cards.pedigreeFull: April Dunford (*Obviously Awesome*, 2019). Developed within enterprise technology product marketing to break corporate over-reliance on aspirational vision statements by grounding positioning in actual customer behavior.
cards.artifactFull: A 5-Column Positioning Ledger mapping Competitive Alternatives \-\> Unique Capabilities \-\> Quantified Value Drivers \-\> Ideal Customer Profile (ICP) Segments \-\> Category Framing.
cards.trapFull: Declaring that "no direct competitors exist" or positioning into expansive, ill-defined spaces (e.g., "the intelligent enterprise layer"), depriving buyers of an evaluative frame of reference.

cards.name: Kapferer’s Brand Identity Prism
cards.diagnostic: How do our external physical codes and relational behaviors mirror the internal culture of our organization and the aspirational self-image of our buyer?
artifact: A six-facet identity prism: Physique, Personality, Culture, Relationship, Reflection, Self-Image.
cards.trap: An identity built entirely on Reflection: customer-pandering marketing with no operational or cultural grounding.
cards.pedigreeFull: Jean-Noël Kapferer (*Strategic Brand Management*, 1992). An academic formulation asserting that a brand exists as a hexagonal prism balanced along externalization-internalization and sender-receiver axes.
cards.artifactFull: A Hexagonal Identity Prism Matrix articulating six structural facets: Physique (visual and physical cues), Personality (character profile), Culture (ideological values), Relationship (mode of interaction), Reflection (perceived target customer), and Self-Image (the customer's internal identity affirmation).
cards.trapFull: Constructing an identity focused entirely on "Reflection," creating customer-pandering marketing that lacks internal operational or cultural grounding.

cards.name: Keller’s Customer-Based Brand Equity (CBBE) Pyramid
cards.diagnostic: Have we established sufficient brand salience and performance credibility to support an emotional brand response and active consumer resonance?
artifact: A four-tier equity ladder: Salience, Performance & Imagery, Judgments & Feelings, Resonance.
cards.trap: Buying resonance campaigns before functional performance and category salience are established: hollow recognition, no conversion.
cards.pedigreeFull: Kevin Lane Keller (Journal of Marketing, 1993; *Strategic Brand Management*, 2001). A four-tier cognitive hierarchy modeling the sequential construction of brand equity in long-term human memory.
cards.artifactFull: A 4-Tier CBBE Stratification Ladder dividing brand equity into: Salience (deep category identity), Performance & Imagery (brand meaning), Judgments & Feelings (brand response), and Resonance (active, loyal psychological attachment).
cards.trapFull: Launching high-budget emotional resonance campaigns before achieving baseline functional performance and category salience, leading to hollow recognition without commercial conversion.

cards.name: Blue Ocean Strategy Canvas & ERRC Grid
cards.diagnostic: Which category conventions can we discard, which must we reduce below standard, and which neglected factors should we elevate to break industry trade-offs?
artifact: A Strategic Value Curve Chart paired with an Eliminate-Reduce-Raise-Create (ERRC) Operational Matrix mapping asymmetric investment against industry benchmarks.
cards.trap: Benchmark convergence: competing on every established axis drives up marginal cost and ends in commoditization.
cards.pedigreeFull: W. Chan Kim & Renée Mauborgne (*Blue Ocean Strategy*, 2005; INSEAD). An analytical framework designed to break the structural trade-off between differentiation and low cost by reconstructing buyer value curves.
cards.artifactFull: A Strategic Value Curve Chart paired with an Eliminate-Reduce-Raise-Create (ERRC) Operational Matrix mapping asymmetric investment against industry benchmarks.
cards.trapFull: Engaging in benchmark convergence—competing simultaneously on every established feature axis, which drives up marginal costs and degrades into a race toward commoditization.

cards.name: Unilever Brand Key
cards.diagnostic: What foundational root strengths and underlying human insights give the brand the commercial authority to claim its core discriminator?
artifact: The 9-Element Brand Key Blueprint: Root Strength \-\> Competitive Environment \-\> Target Audience \-\> Human Insight \-\> Benefits (Functional & Emotional) \-\> Values & Personality \-\> Reasons to Believe (RTB) \-\> Discriminator \-\> Brand Essence.
cards.trap: Writing the Human Insight as an obvious functional observation instead of the underlying psychological tension.
cards.pedigreeFull: Unilever Global Marketing Practice (developed c. 1995). A standardized model deployed across multinational consumer brands to maintain strategic discipline across global agency rosters.
cards.artifactFull: The 9-Element Brand Key Blueprint: Root Strength \-\> Competitive Environment \-\> Target Audience \-\> Human Insight \-\> Benefits (Functional & Emotional) \-\> Values & Personality \-\> Reasons to Believe (RTB) \-\> Discriminator \-\> Brand Essence.
cards.trapFull: Formulating the "Human Insight" as an obvious functional observation (e.g., "developers want faster builds") rather than uncovering the underlying psychological tension.

cards.name: Treacy & Wiersema’s Value Disciplines
cards.diagnostic: Are we positioned primarily around Operational Excellence (cost, reliability, efficiency), Product Leadership (continuous innovation, status), or Customer Intimacy (tailored flexibility, relationship depth)?
artifact: A Value Trilemma Optimization Map establishing a primary operational focus alongside non-negotiable performance thresholds for the other two disciplines.
cards.trap: Promising market-leading craftsmanship, lowest category pricing, and bespoke personalization simultaneously, which confuses operational priorities.
cards.pedigreeFull: Michael Treacy & Fred Wiersema (*The Discipline of Market Leaders*, 1993; Harvard Business Review). A corporate strategy framework asserting that market leaders optimize for exactly one operating dimension while maintaining baseline thresholds in the remaining two.
cards.artifactFull: A Value Trilemma Optimization Map establishing a primary operational focus alongside non-negotiable performance thresholds for the other two disciplines.
cards.trapFull: Promising market-leading craftsmanship, lowest category pricing, and bespoke personalization simultaneously, which confuses operational priorities.

cards.name: Trout & Ries Positioning & Category Law
cards.diagnostic: What single word, category rung, or pre-existing cognitive bias does our brand own to the exclusion of all competitors?
artifact: A Category Ladder Ledger detailing: the Top-of-Mind Category Leader, the Antithetical Second-Rung Position (the "un-leader"), and a Singular Word Association Register.
cards.trap: Diluting a focused mental position by stretching the brand name across unrelated market segments and products.
cards.pedigreeFull: Al Ries & Jack Trout (*Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind*, 1981). The foundational media-era advertising framework that defines positioning as the cognitive ownership of a singular idea in the mind of the prospect.
cards.artifactFull: A Category Ladder Ledger detailing: the Top-of-Mind Category Leader, the Antithetical Second-Rung Position (the "un-leader"), and a Singular Word Association Register.
cards.trapFull: Diluting a focused mental position by stretching the brand name across unrelated market segments and products.

cards.name: The Brand Essence Wheel
cards.diagnostic: When outer technical facts and user benefits are distilled inward, what two-to-three word essence captures the central promise of the brand?
artifact: A 5-Ring Concentric Essence Wheel moving inward from Physical Attributes & Facts to Functional Benefits, Emotional Payoffs, Personality Archetypes, and the central Brand Essence.
cards.trap: Choosing an interchangeable abstraction for the essence — Trust, Innovation, Quality — which carries zero competitive tension.

origin.line: Bates Worldwide / Richard Macrae & Robin Wensley (1990s)

cards.pedigreeFull: Bates Worldwide / Richard Macrae & Robin Wensley (1990s). An advertising agency framework designed to distill multifaceted product offerings down into an unambiguous emotional and functional core.
cards.artifactFull: A 5-Ring Concentric Essence Wheel moving inward from Physical Attributes & Facts to Functional Benefits, Emotional Payoffs, Personality Archetypes, and the central Brand Essence.
cards.trapFull: Selecting an interchangeable corporate abstraction for the core essence (such as "Trust," "Innovation," or "Quality") that offers zero competitive tension.

cards.name: The Brand Onion Model
cards.diagnostic: How do our daily visual and verbal touchpoints connect directly back to our non-negotiable core values and foundational convictions?
artifact: A Multi-Tiered Behavioral Onion Map: Core Values \-\> Brand Essence \-\> Character & Positioning \-\> External Expressions and Manifestations.
cards.trap: Treating the outer behavioral layer as a styling exercise while leaving the core values too broad to guide real business trade-offs.
cards.pedigreeFull: Consumer Goods Strategy Practice (1990s). A diagnostic system that peels back organizational layers to reveal the enduring core identity beneath external marketing expressions.
cards.artifactFull: A Multi-Tiered Behavioral Onion Map: Core Values \-\> Brand Essence \-\> Character & Positioning \-\> External Expressions and Manifestations.
cards.trapFull: Treating the outer behavioral layer as a styling exercise while leaving the core values too broad to guide real business trade-offs.

cards.name: Geoffrey Moore’s Crossing the Chasm Positioning Template
cards.diagnostic: Can our leadership team state our fundamental commercial position in a single sentence using a fixed, adjective-free syntax?
artifact: For [target customer segment]
Who [statement of specific need or pain]
The [product name] is a [product category]
That [statement of compelling key benefit]
Unlike [primary competitive alternative]
Our product [statement of primary differentiation].
cards.trap: Overloading the clauses with buzzwords, which breaks the framework's forcing function.
cards.pedigreeFull: Geoffrey A. Moore (*Crossing the Chasm*, 1991). A structural framework designed for technology markets shifting from visionary early adopters to pragmatic mainstream buyers.
cards.artifactFull:
A Structured Positioning Statement:  
  - For \[target customer segment\]  
  - Who \[statement of specific need or pain\]  
  - The \[product name\] is a \[product category\]  
  - That \[statement of compelling key benefit\]  
  - Unlike \[primary competitive alternative\]  
  - Our product \[statement of primary differentiation\].
cards.trapFull: Overloading clauses with corporate buzzwords (e.g., "For *innovative teams* who *need efficiency*, our *AI-powered engine*..."), which undermines the framework's forcing function.

cards.name: Christensen’s Jobs-to-be-Done (JTBD) Brand Placement
cards.diagnostic: What functional, emotional, and social 'job' is the customer hiring our brand to resolve, and what incumbent habits or solutions must be 'fired'?
artifact: A JTBD Forces of Progress Blueprint mapping the push of the current situation, the pull of the new solution, the anxiety of change, and the inertia of existing habits.
cards.trap: Defining the brand's addressable market solely through demographic profiles rather than the situational triggers that drive buying decisions.

origin.line: Clayton M. Christensen, Scott Cook & Taddy Hall (2016)

cards.pedigreeFull: Clayton M. Christensen, Scott Cook, & Taddy Hall (*Competing Against Luck*, 2016; Harvard Business School). A theory asserting that customers purchase solutions to make progress against specific, recurring life situations.
cards.artifactFull: A JTBD Forces of Progress Blueprint mapping the push of the current situation, the pull of the new solution, the anxiety of change, and the inertia of existing habits.
cards.trapFull: Defining the brand's addressable market solely through demographic profiles rather than the situational triggers that drive buying decisions.

cards.name: Pearson-Jung 12 Brand Archetypes
cards.diagnostic: Which universal subconscious archetype governs our brand's behavioral defaults, motivation, and cultural stance?
artifact: Two axes (Stability vs. Disruption; Belonging vs. Autonomy) yield a primary and a secondary archetype, with core drivers, fears and taboos.
cards.trap: Picking an archetype as decoration while operations contradict its ethos — an *Outlaw* run under strict risk aversion.
cards.pedigreeFull: Carol S. Pearson & Margaret Mark (*The Hero and the Outlaw*, 2001), adapting Carl G. Jung’s psychoanalytic theory of collective archetypes.
cards.artifactFull: An Archetypal Persona Specification mapping the brand across two psychological axes (Stability vs. Disruption; Belonging vs. Autonomy) into a Primary Archetype (e.g., *Sage*) and Secondary Archetype (e.g., *Creator*), complete with core drivers, fears, and taboos.
cards.trapFull: Selecting an archetype as a surface-level marketing exercise while running operations in direct contradiction to that archetype's ethos (e.g., claiming to be an *Outlaw* while operating under strict corporate risk aversion).

cards.name: Aaker’s Brand Personality Dimensions
cards.diagnostic: How does the brand score across the five validated psychological dimensions, and which sub-facets serve as non-negotiable behavioral boundaries?
artifact: A 42-Facet Personality Trait Scorecard evaluating the brand on a 1–5 scale across five primary dimensions: Sincerity, Excitement, Competence, Sophistication, and Ruggedness.
cards.trap: Scoring high across all five dimensions simultaneously, resulting in a diffuse identity profile that dilutes recognition.
cards.pedigreeFull: Jennifer L. Aaker (Journal of Marketing Research, 1997). The foundational empirical psychometric model validating how human personality traits project onto commercial brands.
cards.artifactFull: A 42-Facet Personality Trait Scorecard evaluating the brand on a 1–5 scale across five primary dimensions: Sincerity, Excitement, Competence, Sophistication, and Ruggedness.
cards.trapFull: Scoring high across all five dimensions simultaneously, resulting in a diffuse identity profile that dilutes recognition.

cards.name: Nielsen Norman Group (NN/g) 4 Dimensions of Tone of Voice
cards.diagnostic: Where does our content fall along the four universal tonal axes across different user states and contexts?
artifact: Four bipolar axes — Funny↔Serious, Formal↔Casual, Respectful↔Irreverent, Matter-of-Fact↔Enthusiastic — each with copy treatments across onboarding, core tasks and system errors.
cards.trap: Staying playful through critical failures — a failed transaction, a locked account — alienates users already under stress.
cards.pedigreeFull: Nielsen Norman Group (Kate Moran, 2016). A digital user experience research framework that isolates verbal identity into four bipolar, actionable dimensions.
cards.artifactFull: A 4-Axis Bipolar Tone Matrix: Funny \<-\> Serious; Formal \<-\> Casual; Respectful \<-\> Irreverent; Matter-of-Fact \<-\> Enthusiastic, supported by practical copy treatments across onboarding, core tasks, and system errors.
cards.trapFull: Adopting an irreverent or playful tone during critical product failures (e.g., failed transactions, authentication locks), which alienates users under stress.

cards.name: Brand Personality Appeal (BPA) Model
cards.diagnostic: Is our brand personality distinct enough to be recognized, favorable enough to drive preference, and clear enough to prevent internal misinterpretation?
artifact: A three-factor audit: Personality Favorability, Personality Originality, Personality Clarity.
cards.trap: Chasing originality that fails favorability: eccentricities added for novelty raise friction at adoption.

origin.line: Traci H. Freling, Jody L. Crosno & David H. Henard (2011)

cards.pedigreeFull: Traci H. Freling, Jody L. Crosno, & David H. Henard (Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science, 2011). An academic model assessing the structural efficacy of a brand personality on consumer behavior.
cards.artifactFull: A BPA Commercial Resonance Audit measuring three empirical factors: Personality Favorability (net positive sentiment impact), Personality Originality (differentiation from category baselines), and Personality Clarity (consistency of external perception).
cards.trapFull: Pursuing an original brand personality that fails the favorability test—introducing eccentricities purely for novelty that add friction to buyer adoption.

cards.name: Jungian Shadow Archetypes in Enterprise Culture
cards.diagnostic: What toxic behavioral shadow does our primary archetype risk becoming when our organization is placed under commercial pressure, and what structural safeguards prevent its manifestation?
artifact: A shadow register: the primary archetype, the state it becomes under pressure (*Hero* → *Arrogant Bully*; *Sage* → *Pedantic Academic*; *Ruler* → *Authoritarian Tyrant*), and the policies that prevent it.
cards.trap: Ignoring shadow states during high-growth cycles, allowing latent behaviors to turn public marketing campaigns into brand crises.

origin.line: Carl G. Jung, applied by Pearson & Mark (2001)

cards.pedigreeFull: Derived from Carl G. Jung’s analytical psychology (*The Shadow*, 1951\) and applied to corporate culture by Pearson and Mark. The framework posits that every dominant archetype contains an unintegrated, destructive shadow state that surfaces under stress.
cards.artifactFull: An Archetypal Crisis & Shadow Register detailing the primary archetype, its potential shadow state (e.g., *Hero* becoming *Arrogant Bully*; *Sage* becoming *Pedantic Academic*; *Ruler* becoming *Authoritarian Tyrant*), and organizational preventative policies.
cards.trapFull: Ignoring shadow states during high-growth cycles, allowing latent behaviors to turn public marketing campaigns into brand crises.

cards.name: Five-Factor (OCEAN) Brand Mapping
cards.diagnostic: If evaluated through standardized psychometric testing, what exact trait distribution governs our corporate communications?
artifact: A radar chart scoring the five factors: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism.
cards.trap: Mirroring the founder's uncalibrated traits instead of engineering the profile the target market requires.

origin.line: Gian Vittorio Caprara, Claudio Barbaranelli & Gianluigi Guido (2001)

cards.pedigreeFull: Gian Vittorio Caprara, Claudio Barbaranelli, & Gianluigi Guido (Journal of Economic Psychology, 2001). Adaptation of the gold-standard Costa & McCrae Big Five psychometric model (Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism) to enterprise positioning.
cards.artifactFull: An OCEAN Polar Radar Chart scoring Openness to Experience (intellectual curiosity), Conscientiousness (operational reliability), Extraversion (conversational assertiveness), Agreeableness (empathy and support), and Neuroticism (environmental volatility and urgency).
cards.trapFull: Mirroring the executive founder's uncalibrated personal traits rather than engineering the deliberate behavioral profile required by the target market.

cards.name: The Brand Voice Compass & Sliders
cards.diagnostic: What specific lexical, structural, and grammatical rules define each of our brand personality traits in practical writing?
artifact: Trait Name
Positive Definition: what the trait actively is
Negative Boundary: what it must never become
Side-by-side "Use This / Avoid That" copy examples
cards.trap: Listing broad adjectives — Bold, Smart, Human — with no boundaries, leaving copywriters nothing to act on.
cards.pedigreeFull: Modern verbal identity systems practice (derived from digital design system and docs-as-code methodologies).
cards.artifactFull:
A Verbal Compass & Governance Guide defining:  
  - Trait Name  
  - Positive Definition (what the trait actively is)  
  - Negative Boundary (what the trait must never become)  
  - Side-by-side "Use This / Avoid That" copy examples.
cards.trapFull: Listing broad tonal adjectives (such as "Bold," "Smart," or "Human") without defining concrete boundaries, leaving copywriters without actionable constraints.

cards.name: Dialectical Tonal Polarity Matrix
cards.diagnostic: What opposing behavioral tensions must our brand balance to avoid collapsing into a flat, predictable stereotype?
artifact: Trait tensions: *Deeply Technical* yet *Instantly Plainspoken*; *Pragmatic and Grounded* yet *Uncompromisingly Visionary*.
Calibration bounds marking the point where each extreme turns destructive.
cards.trap: Resolving the tension by softening both sides toward a bland middle ground, erasing distinctiveness.
cards.pedigreeFull: Dialectical philosophy applied to communications architecture, establishing brand identity through the dynamic resolution of opposing traits.
cards.artifactFull:
A Dialectical Tonal Guardrail Matrix:  
  - Trait Tensions: e.g., *Deeply Technical* yet *Instantly Plainspoken*; *Pragmatic and Grounded* yet *Uncompromisingly Visionary*.  
  - Operational calibration bounds marking the points where each extreme turns destructive.
cards.trapFull: Resolving the tension by softening both sides toward a bland middle ground, erasing distinctiveness.

cards.name: Fournier’s Brand Relationship Quality (BRQ) Model
cards.diagnostic: What specific relational contract does our brand form with the customer, and do our operational touchpoints reinforce or break that contract?
artifact: Six facets — Love/Passion, Self-Connection, Interdependence, Commitment, Intimacy, Brand Partner Quality — scored across relationship archetypes such as Committed Partnership or Secret Fling.
cards.trap: Using an intimate, conversational tone when the business reality is an opportunistic transaction reads as false.
cards.pedigreeFull: Susan Fournier (Journal of Consumer Research, 1998). An academic framework analyzing consumer-brand connections as active socio-emotive relationships.
cards.artifactFull: A 6-Facet Relational Typology Map evaluating Love/Passion, Self-Connection, Interdependence, Commitment, Intimacy, and Brand Partner Quality across relationship archetypes (e.g., Committed Partnership, Marriage of Convenience, Childhood Friendship, Secret Fling).
cards.trapFull: Adopting an intimate, conversational tone in marketing when the underlying business reality is an opportunistic transaction, triggering customer skepticism.

cards.name: Greimasian Brand Semiotic Square
cards.diagnostic: What structural oppositions and contradictions define the narrative space of our category, and what unexplored territory can we claim?
artifact: A 4-Corner Structural Semiotic Matrix: Primary Assertion (S1) vs. Contrary (S2), and Contradictory (~ S1) vs. Sub-Contrary (~ S2), mapping category positions and white space.
cards.trap: Positioning a brand on an unresolved contradictory axis without addressing the underlying semantic trade-offs.

origin.line: Algirdas Julien Greimas (1966), adapted by Jean-Marie Floch (1988)

cards.pedigreeFull: Algirdas Julien Greimas (*Structural Semantics*, 1966\) adapted to corporate semiotics by Jean-Marie Floch (1988). A logical tool that maps out the semantic limits and relationships of meaning within a category.
cards.artifactFull: A 4-Corner Structural Semiotic Matrix: Primary Assertion (\$S\_1\$) vs. Contrary (\$S\_2\$), and Contradictory (\$\\sim S\_1\$) vs. Sub-Contrary (\$\\sim S\_2\$), mapping category positions and white space.
cards.trapFull: Positioning a brand on an unresolved contradictory axis without addressing the underlying semantic trade-offs.
cards.sourceNote: The source writes the four corners in escaped LaTeX (math-mode delimiters around S with subscript markers); the declared rendering table drops those delimiters, so the card prints S1, S2, ~S1, ~S2.

cards.name: Simon Sinek’s Golden Circle
cards.diagnostic: Why does our enterprise exist beyond generating profit, and does that purpose consistently drive our operating principles and product output?
artifact: A Concentric Why-How-What Blueprint: Why (the foundational cause or conviction), How (the proprietary operating principles), and What (the tangible products and services).
cards.trap: Inventing an ungrounded social crusade for a functional utility business, resulting in transparent purpose-washing.
cards.pedigreeFull: Simon Sinek (*Start With Why*, 2009). A teleological model drawing on evolutionary neuroscience, proposing that human decision-making is led by limbic emotion before rational neocortical justification.
cards.artifactFull: A Concentric Why-How-What Blueprint: Why (the foundational cause or conviction), How (the proprietary operating principles), and What (the tangible products and services).
cards.trapFull: Inventing an ungrounded social crusade for a functional utility business, resulting in transparent purpose-washing.

cards.name: The Brand Story Canvas
cards.diagnostic: How does our brand narrative guide the customer through their struggle against an obstacle toward an altered state of success?
artifact: A Single-Page Strategic Storyboard: Protagonist \-\> Inciting Incident \-\> External/Internal Conflict \-\> The Guide \-\> The Action Plan \-\> The Climax \-\> The New Status Quo.
cards.trap: Making the company the hero of the story rather than positioning the customer as the protagonist and the brand as the guide.
cards.pedigreeFull: Narrative systems practice, translating classical dramatic screenwriting structures into corporate strategy design.
cards.artifactFull: A Single-Page Strategic Storyboard tracking: Protagonist \-\> Inciting Incident \-\> External/Internal Conflict \-\> The Guide \-\> The Action Plan \-\> The Climax \-\> The New Status Quo.
cards.trapFull: Making the company the hero of the story rather than positioning the customer as the protagonist and the brand as the guide.

cards.name: Purpose-Mission-Vision-Values (PMVV) Alignment Hierarchy
cards.diagnostic: Are our Purpose, Mission, Vision, and Values structurally delineated, or do they collapse into a single corporate statement?
artifact: *Purpose*: the enduring reason for being (permanent).
*Mission*: the high-priority operational objective over a 3–5 year horizon (dynamic).
*Vision*: the future market state realized once the mission succeeds (long-term).
*Values*: the boundaries that will not be compromised, even at a financial loss (ethical).
cards.trap: Adopting generic corporate hygiene factors — Integrity, Excellence, Teamwork — as values without defining the trade-offs they require.

origin.line: Peter Drucker; Jim Collins & Jerry Porras (1994)

cards.pedigreeFull: Classical strategic management practice (Peter Drucker; Jim Collins & Jerry Porras, *Built to Last*, 1994).
cards.artifactFull:
A Four-Tier Institutional Architecture:  
  - *Purpose:* The organization's enduring reason for being (permanent).  
  - *Mission:* The immediate, high-priority operational objective over a 3–5 year horizon (dynamic).  
  - *Vision:* The future market state realized once the mission succeeds (long-term).  
  - *Values:* The operational boundaries that will not be compromised, even at a financial loss (ethical).
cards.trapFull: Adopting generic corporate hygiene factors (e.g., "Integrity," "Excellence," "Teamwork") as core values without defining the trade-offs they require.
cards.sourceNote: The source names Drucker with no work or year and Collins & Porras with one; the card prints what the source gives and adds nothing.

cards.name: The Enemy/Rival Category Narrative
cards.diagnostic: What systemic injustice, flawed industry consensus, or operational failure serves as our brand's philosophical antagonist?
artifact: An Antagonist Dossier & Contrarian Manifesto: the systemic adversary (e.g., *The Fragmentation of Data*, *Vendor Lock-in*), the impact on the customer, and the brand's path to overcoming it.
cards.trap: Targeting a specific corporate competitor by name, which can appear petty and reduces the brand's category leadership.

origin.line: Play Bigger (2016); Alex M. H. Smith (2020)

cards.pedigreeFull: Category design theory and narrative strategy (*Play Bigger*, 2016; Alex M. H. Smith, 2020).
cards.artifactFull: An Antagonist Dossier & Contrarian Manifesto detailing the systemic adversary (e.g., *The Fragmentation of Data*, *Vendor Lock-in*), the impact on the customer, and the brand's path to overcoming it.
cards.trapFull: Targeting a specific corporate competitor by name, which can appear petty and reduces the brand's category leadership.
cards.sourceNote: The source cites Play Bigger (2016) without its authors and Alex M. H. Smith (2020) as the second origin; the card prints the source's line and does not add the authors.

cards.name: Andy Raskin’s 5-Element Strategic Narrative
cards.diagnostic: Does our narrative open with an undeniable shift in the macro environment that creates urgency, or are we leading with self-centered product pitches?
artifact: Name an undeniable shift in the world.
Demonstrate there will be winners and losers (the stakes).
Tease the promised land — the future state, independent of features.
Introduce product capabilities as "magic gifts" to reach that state.
Present concrete evidence that the vision can be realized.
cards.trap: Opening with a slide that tells the prospect their current approach is broken, which triggers immediate resistance.
cards.pedigreeFull: Andy Raskin (*The Greatest Sales Deck I’ve Ever Seen*, 2016), adapted from Hollywood screenwriting principles for business-to-business enterprise narratives.
cards.artifactFull:
A 5-Stage Narrative Sales Architecture:  
  1. Name an Undeniable Shift in the World  
  2. Demonstrate There Will Be Winners and Losers (The Stakes)  
  3. Tease the Promised Land (The future state, independent of features)  
  4. Introduce Product Capabilities as "Magic Gifts" to Reach That State  
  5. Present Concrete Evidence Proving the Vision Can Be Realized.
cards.trapFull: Starting a sales pitch with a slide claiming the prospect's current approach is broken, which triggers immediate psychological resistance.

cards.name: Donald Miller’s StoryBrand Framework (SB7)
cards.diagnostic: Can an uninformed user understand what we offer, what problem it resolves, and how to buy it within five seconds of landing on our touchpoint?
artifact: A 7-Part Grunt-Tested BrandScript: Character \-\> Problem (External, Internal, Philosophical) \-\> Guide (Empathy \+ Authority) \-\> Plan \-\> Call to Action \-\> Avoided Failure \-\> Resulting Success.
cards.trap: Cluttering above-the-fold messaging with internal corporate milestones, history, or technical jargon rather than clarifying user progress.
cards.pedigreeFull: Donald Miller (*Building a StoryBrand*, 2017). A narrative structure derived from classic screenwriting designed to eliminate cognitive noise in marketing.
cards.artifactFull: A 7-Part Grunt-Tested BrandScript: Character \-\> Problem (External, Internal, Philosophical) \-\> Guide (Empathy \+ Authority) \-\> Plan \-\> Call to Action \-\> Avoided Failure \-\> Resulting Success.
cards.trapFull: Cluttering above-the-fold messaging with internal corporate milestones, history, or technical jargon rather than clarifying user progress.

cards.name: Campbellian Monomyth Brand Adaptation
cards.diagnostic: What threshold of change is our customer hesitant to cross, and how does our brand serve as the mentor providing the tools to succeed?
artifact: A 12-stage journey map: Ordinary World, Call to Adventure, Refusal of the Call, Meeting the Mentor, Crossing the Threshold, Tests/Allies/Enemies, Inmost Cave, Supreme Ordeal, Reward, The Road Back, Resurrection, Return with the Elixir.
cards.trap: Melodramatizing low-involvement or routine purchases, alienating practical buyers.
cards.pedigreeFull: Joseph Campbell (*The Hero with a Thousand Faces*, 1949), adapted for modern narrative analysis by Christopher Vogler (*The Writer’s Journey*, 1992).
cards.artifactFull: A 12-Stage Customer Journey Map tracking the Ordinary World, Call to Adventure, Refusal of the Call, Meeting the Mentor, Crossing the Threshold, Tests/Allies/Enemies, Inmost Cave, Supreme Ordeal, Reward, The Road Back, Resurrection, and Return with the Elixir.
cards.trapFull: Melodramatizing low-involvement or routine purchases, alienating practical buyers.

cards.name: McKee’s Storynomics Narrative Engine
cards.diagnostic: What unexpected event breaks our customer's status quo, and what progressive gaps between expectation and reality must they navigate?
artifact: An Expectation-Gap Narrative Graph: Baseline Equilibrium \-\> Inciting Incident \-\> Object of Desire \-\> Action \-\> Gap (Expectation vs. Reality) \-\> Escalating Conflict \-\> Decisive Crisis \-\> Re-established Equilibrium.
cards.trap: Presenting an idealized, friction-free customer journey that fails to acknowledge real implementation obstacles.

cards.name: Romaniuk’s Distinctive Brand Asset (DBA) Grid
cards.diagnostic: What proportion of market buyers correctly associate our non-logo assets with our brand, and what proportion mistakenly attribute them to a competitor?
artifact: Two axes: Fame (share of buyers linking the asset to the brand) and Uniqueness (share associating it only with the brand).
*Automatic* (high fame / high uniqueness): strong enough to replace the logo.
*Investment Potential* (low fame / high uniqueness): needs broad media reinforcement.
*Avoid Solo Use* (high fame / low uniqueness): prompts competitor recall alone.
*Ignore or Test* (low fame / low uniqueness): drains marketing resources.
cards.trap: Redesigning established assets because the internal team is bored, which destroys earned market memory.
cards.pedigreeFull: Jenni Romaniuk & Byron Sharp (Ehrenberg-Bass Institute; *Building Distinctive Brand Assets*, 2018).
cards.artifactFull:
A 4-Quadrant DBA Resource Matrix categorizing non-logo brand assets across two empirical axes: Fame (% of buyers who link the asset to the brand) and Uniqueness (% of responses that associate the asset exclusively with the brand):  
  - *Automatic (High Fame / High Uniqueness):* Assets strong enough to replace the logo entirely.  
  - *Investment Potential (Low Fame / High Uniqueness):* Assets requiring broad media reinforcement.  
  - *Avoid Solo Use (High Fame / Low Uniqueness):* Assets that prompt competitor recall if used alone.  
  - *Ignore or Test (Low Fame / Low Uniqueness):* Low-value assets that drain marketing resources.
cards.trapFull: Redesigning well-established brand assets simply because internal creative teams have grown bored with them, destroying hard-earned market memory structures.
